2.text: the Koryak in 1745. The first priests in both countries belonged to the

3.text: family of Trifonov. Thus, we find in Nishne-Kolymsk, in the year 1753, the

4.text: priest Michael Trifonov. This priest was the sole one for the whole country,

5.text: and had to visit all three of the Kolyma towns; and before that he was

6.text: priest of the Anadyr Chukchee. In 1757 we find another priest, Procope

7.text: Trifonov, who was transferred to Anadyr in 1758; but in 1764, after the

8.text: abolishment of the fortress of Anadyrsk, he was restored to his former place.

9.text: In 1812, with the new trade-regulations, the priest of Nishne-Kolymsk

10.text: received a new nomination as a Chukchee missionary. The name of this

11.text: first missionary was Gregory Slieptzov. He remained in his former parish,

12.text: however, and only had to visit the Anui fair once a year. Argentov mentions

13.text: that in 1811-12 Slieptzov made a trip to the Chaun country. The next “parish

14.text: missionary,” A. Trifonov, who went to the Kolyma in 1816, has never visited

15.text: the Chukchee. In his time the Archbishop of Irkutsk, Michael, wrote an

16.text: epistle to the Chukchee, exhorting them to adopt Christianity (1818). I wonder

17.text: how many Chukchee have read the said epistle!

18.text: In 1848, at the instance of Archbishop Nil, a small church was built

19.text: on the Arctic shore at the mouth of Big River (Large Baranikha River),

20.text: two hundred miles from Nishne-Kolymsk, and A. Argentov was appointed the

21.text: first missionary. It seems that before that he had been an ordinary priest

22.text: on the Lower Kolyma for more than four years. He says in his diary that

23.text: the place was selected not very happily, because the Chukchee do not live

24.text: there continually, but only come from time to time. This, of course, is quite

25.text: true. Nevertheless Argentov went to his church along the seacoast with five

26.text: boats of the usual Kolyma type. These boats are so clumsy and fragile that

27.text: it is a matter of wonder that the expedition did not meet with some catas-

28.text: trophe. The people who came in the boats built a block-house for Argentov,

29.text: and then went back, leaving him with his wife and a maid-servant. A few

30.text: months after that Argentov was obliged to flee from his mission, because the

31.text: Chukchee neighbors wanted to compel him to enter with them into a bond

32.text: of group-marriage. The story is well remembered on the Kolyma among the

33.text: Russians as well as among the Chukchee. Argentov, who travelled much

34.text: among the Chukchee, and visited Chaun River and Cape Erri, was tempted

35.text: to conclude friendship with one Chukchee, Ataˊto, and also with his wife.

36.text: Probably at that time he did not know the rules of the Chukchee group-

37.text: marriage; but after a short time Ataˊto returned the visit, and asked for

38.text: reciprocity. He had some companions with him, and so refusal was of no

39.text: avail. At the critical moment, however, the maid-servant consented to take

40.text: the place of the mistress. The Chukchee probably did not know the difference;

41.text: and, moreover, according to Chukchee ideas, the family has a right, in marriage

42.text: complications, to substitute one woman for another. Some of these details I

43.text: have from Ataˊto himself, who in 1895 was still living. Shortly after that,
